# Multi-Rate Systems Hierarchy\chaptersubtitle{Decoupling Cognitive Speeds Across Heterogeneous Silicon} {#sec-hierarchy}

![**Systems Organ Focus: The Multi-Rate Temporal Hierarchy and the Proposal–Permission Boundary.** Decoupling slow, non-deterministic foundation models from deterministic, bare-metal safety reflexes across physical constraints.](figures/fig_pipeline_locator.svg){#fig-locator-ch04 fig-pos="H" width=100%}

*How do we bridge the massive temporal gap between a slow, stochastic foundation model and a microsecond-deterministic motor reflex without crashing the machine?*

In classical computing, software is decoupled from physical time. If a foundation model stalls and its inference latency spikes from 200 milliseconds to 2 seconds, the digital universe patiently waits behind glass. A loading spinner appears, but nothing breaks. In Physical AI, however, time is an unyielding dynamical coordinate. While an algorithm deliberates in silicon, inertia carries moving linkages forward, gravity accelerates ungrounded masses, and sensory observations rapidly decay toward obsolescence. If your computational pipeline fails to deliver valid actuation commands before physical reality diverges from internal belief, the result is mechanical collision and structural failure.

2. **Dissect Cadence Failures:** Perform a forensic autopsy of the Tempe automated vehicle collision, tracing how classification jitter and software suppression delays consumed dynamic stopping margins.
3. **Partition Heterogeneous Silicon:** Map cognitive cadences across Application Processors (Linux MPUs), Neural Accelerators (Edge NPUs), and Real-Time Microcontrollers (Bare-Metal MCUs).
4. **Enforce the Proposal–Permission Boundary:** Separate unverified neural model proposals from deterministic hardware authority.
5. **Implement Expiring Intent Leases:** Author formal intent contracts ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{intent}}$) bounded by spatial validity hulls and hardware watchdog timers.
6. **Navigate the Master Co-Design Matrix:** Evaluate systems tensions across the 5×5 Physical Agent Co-Design Matrix to guide full-stack engineering.
7. **Architect Zero-Allocation Inter-Cadence IPC:** Design lock-free SRAM ring buffers using atomic sequence counters and zero dynamic heap allocation (`malloc = 0`).

**Core Chapter Takeaway:** Embodied intelligence cannot execute as a single monolithic software loop; it demands an asynchronous multi-rate hierarchy that decouples slow foundation models from deterministic, bare-metal safety reflexes across a strict Proposal–Permission boundary.

## The Multi-Rate Imperative

The defining engineering challenge of Physical AI is not simply model size or algorithmic sophistication; it is **physical time** (@fig-locator-ch04). 

In conventional computing, software execution is decoupled from the passage of physical time. If a cloud-based foundation model experiences an operating system scheduling stall, memory garbage collection pause, or network socket timeout, the digital universe patiently waits behind glass. A loading spinner appears on screen, but nothing breaks. In the physical universe, however, time is an unyielding dynamical coordinate. While an algorithm deliberates in silicon, moving mass carries kinetic momentum forward ($p = mv$), gravity accelerates ungrounded linkages, and sensory observations rapidly decay into obsolescence. If computational pipelines fail to deliver valid actuation commands before physical reality diverges from internal belief, the result is mechanical destruction.

This reality creates what this chapter terms the **Cadence Chasm**: the four-order-of-magnitude temporal mismatch between the slow, stochastic deliberation of deep foundation models and the microsecond-deterministic reflexes required to stabilize physical hardware:

* **The Deliberative Tier ($0.5\text{--}2\text{ Hz}$):** Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models scaling to tens of billions of parameters perform open-world semantic scene understanding, task decomposition, and symbolic reasoning. These models execute billions of floating-point operations over stochastic, autoregressive decoding loops, requiring hundreds to thousands of milliseconds per forward pass.
* **The Trajectory Tier ($20\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$):** Neural trajectory decoders, diffusion policies, and Model Predictive Control (MPC) optimizers convert macroscopic semantic goals into continuous joint waypoint trajectories, operating at dozens of Hertz on dedicated neural accelerators.
* **The Reflex Tier ($1000\text{ Hz}$):** Contact impedance controllers, dynamic safety barrier enforcers, and joint state observers executing at a deterministic $1000\text{ Hz}$ ($1.0\text{ ms} \pm 5\,\mu\text{s}$) to compute torque and impedance setpoints for downstream $10\text{--}40\text{ kHz}$ Field-Oriented Control (FOC) motor inverter stages, reject external disturbances, and enforce physical clearance envelopes.

Attempting to force these radically different timescales into a single monolithic software loop, such as a single synchronous `while True:` script that captures camera frames, queries a foundation model, calculates splines, and commands motor voltages, is an architectural defect known as the *while-loop catastrophe*. In a monolithic loop, high-frequency motor control is artificially yoked to the worst-case tail latency ($P_{99.9} > 1500\text{ ms}$) of the slowest, most non-deterministic neural inference thread. A single operating system memory compaction pause or transformer inference stall pauses the motor commutation loop (the microsecond-level electronic switching of stator phase currents), starving the actuators of updated commands and leaving the physical robot to coast unguided into obstacles.

Overcoming the Cadence Chasm demands an asynchronous, multi-rate temporal hierarchy enforced across heterogeneous silicon. 

To establish this architectural blueprint, this chapter investigates how physical systems bridge cognitive timescales. We begin with a forensic autopsy of the landmark 2018 Tempe autonomous vehicle collision (Section 4.2), demonstrating how classification toggling and an unmanaged one-second suppression timer consumed physical stopping clearance. We then formalize the Three Cadences of Physical AI (Section 4.3), mapping their mathematical requirements, silicon substrates, and frequency-domain stability criteria. Next, we map these cadences across heterogeneous processor cores (Section 4.4), before designing zero-copy lock-free ring buffers in static SRAM (Section 4.5) to exchange trajectory chunks without thread contention. 

We then establish the Proposal–Permission Privilege Split (Section 4.6), confining high-capacity neural networks to unprivileged proposal generators bounded by time-limited intent leases and minimal-intervention safety filters. Finally, we introduce the 5x5 Co-Design Matrix (Section 4.7) to synthesize the foundational principles of Part I, stress-test multi-rate systems engineering through high-stakes Architectural Food for Thought (Section 4.8), and hand off the system blueprint to the sensory-motor organs of Part II (Section 4.9).


## Incident Autopsy: Tempe Desynchronization

To understand why monolithic software execution fails catastrophically when coupled to physical mass, we conduct a forensic autopsy of the formal National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigation into the March 2018 Uber Advanced Technologies Group (ATG) autonomous vehicle collision in Tempe, Arizona. The experimental platform, illustrated in @fig-tempe-testbed, was a modified Volvo XC90 sport utility vehicle operating in autonomous mode, cruising northbound on an unlit multi-lane arterial road at $v = 19.4\text{ m/s}$ ($43.5\text{ mph}$, or approximately $70\text{ km/h}$). In classical computer vision benchmarks, software performance is characterized by abstract statistical metrics such as mean average precision or frame processing throughput; in embodied AI, however, an operating vehicle represents a two-ton physical mass possessing substantial linear kinetic energy ($E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 \approx 3.8 \times 10^5\text{ J}$) traversing physical space in unyielding real time. Every millisecond of algorithmic delay or state corruption burns irreplaceable physical clearance. The Tempe crash was not caused by catastrophic sensor blindness, optical occlusion, or sudden mechanical actuator breakage; rather, it was engineered by an architectural failure of multi-rate systems partitioning, specifically subordinating real-time braking safety authority to a stochastic, asynchronous neural perception loop without enforcing a deterministic Proposal–Permission boundary.

::: {.callout-autopsy title="The Tempe Desynchronization"}

* **System:** Modified Volvo XC90 automated vehicle platform ($m \approx 2100\text{ kg}$) cruising at $v = 19.4\text{ m/s}$ ($43.5\text{ mph}$, $70\text{ km/h}$) on an unlit multi-lane arterial roadway in Tempe, Arizona.
* **Incident:** Autonomous vehicle struck a pedestrian pushing a cargo-laden bicycle across traffic lanes at full cruising velocity with zero automated braking deceleration applied, dissipating $3.8 \times 10^5\text{ J}$ of kinetic energy in a fatal impact.
* **Telemetry Snapshot:** First detected at $T - 5.6\text{ s}$ ($82\text{ m}$ range); classifier toggled across four distinct semantic labels; Kalman filter velocity reset to $\mathbf{0}$ on each label toggle; motion planner asserted $1000\text{ ms}$ suppression delay at $T - 1.2\text{ s}$ ($23.3\text{ m}$ clearance); impact at $T + 0.0\text{ s}$ ($d_{\text{clearance}} = 0\text{ m}$).
* **Root Cause:** Semantic label thrashing in the $10\text{ Hz}$ neural classifier caused the tracking subsystem to repeatedly destruct and re-instantiate C++ tracking objects, zeroing the Kalman filter velocity state vector and hiding lateral motion until an unmanaged $1.0\text{ s}$ software suppression timer burned the remaining physical dynamic stopping clearance.
* **Architectural Flaw:** Monolithic centralization of safety authority within an asynchronous, class-dependent neural perception pipeline rather than delegating emergency stopping to an independent, class-agnostic 1 kHz bare-metal safety reflex.
* **Provenance:** Formal National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigation report NTSB/HAR-19/03 (Accident HWY18MH010).

:::

![**The Uber ATG Automated Driving System Test Platform.** Deploying a modified Volvo XC90 equipped with roof-mounted LiDAR, radar clusters, and optical cameras. The NTSB investigation revealed that asynchronous classification toggling across the $10\text{ Hz}$ perception pipeline repeatedly reset tracking state velocity vectors, while an artificial $1000\text{ ms}$ software suppression delay consumed the physical dynamic stopping margin.](figures/fig03_tempe_vehicle_cropped.jpg){#fig-tempe-testbed width=85%}

The origin of the failure began in the high-level perception pipeline, which ingested 64-beam LiDAR point clouds, radar returns, and multi-camera video streams on an onboard high-performance computing chassis executing at a nominal frequency of $10\text{ Hz}$ ($\Delta t = 100\text{ ms}$). At $T - 5.6\text{ s}$ prior to impact, when the vehicle was $82\text{ m}$ away, the perception system successfully detected an unclassified obstacle in the roadway (a pedestrian pushing an outsized, cargo-laden bicycle across the traffic lanes). Because the pedestrian was crossing an unlit roadway away from a designated crosswalk and exhibited an atypical visual geometry, the deep neural classification backbone lacked high-confidence prior weights for this out-of-distribution morphology. Over the subsequent four seconds, as the vehicle traversed more than $75\text{ m}$ of asphalt, the perception network's categorical softmax distribution (its confidence scores across classes) sat on a razor's edge of epistemic uncertainty, repeatedly thrashing across distinct ontological labels. The model initially categorized the obstacle as an `unknown_vehicle` at $T - 5.6\text{ s}$, flipped the label to `other/static_obstacle` at $T - 4.5\text{ s}$, transitioned to `bicycle` at $T - 2.6\text{ s}$, and subsequently collapsed back to `unknown_object` at $T - 1.5\text{ s}$.

Under standard multi-target tracking theory, an object's spatial kinematics should be decoupled from its semantic label. In legacy object-oriented autonomy architectures, however, tracking entities were implemented as polymorphic C++ class instances under a rigid type-hierarchy assumption where each object class maintained separate kinematic motion models and history queues. Consequently, every time the neural classifier flipped its semantic label at $10\text{ Hz}$, the tracking subsystem did not merely update a Bayesian class posterior; instead, it destructed the existing C++ tracking entity, reallocated a new object in heap memory, wiped the historical state tracking buffer, and initialized the Kalman filter state vector with zero velocity ($\hat{\mathbf{v}} = \mathbf{0}$). In discrete-time Kalman filtering, position $\mathbf{p}_k$ is directly observed, but velocity $\mathbf{v}_k = \dot{\mathbf{p}}$ is a latent state whose estimation covariance $\mathbf{P}_k$ requires multiple consecutive observation updates to converge. By destroying the tracking entity and repeatedly re-initializing $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_0 = [\mathbf{p}_0^T, \mathbf{0}^T]^T$ with an un-converged covariance, the filter was mathematically blinded to the cross-track lateral velocity $\dot{y}$ of the crossing pedestrian. As a result, the forward trajectory projection module assumed the obstacle was stationary along the shoulder rather than traversing across the vehicle's path, projecting a benign path corridor and blinding downstream trajectory planners to the impending geometric collision until $T - 1.2\text{ s}$ before impact.

The cadence collapse was compounded by a fatal software mitigation introduced by the development team to handle sensor false positives: an artificial $1000\text{ ms}$ software suppression delay on emergency braking commands. In dense urban driving, transient neural misclassifications and phantom radar reflections frequently triggered momentary emergency braking pulses, creating severe passenger discomfort and rear-end collision hazards. Rather than addressing the upstream sensor fusion and epistemic uncertainty calibration, software engineers placed an unmanaged user-space timer in the decision pipeline that required emergency braking requests to persist continuously for $1.0\text{ s}$ before dispatching actuation commands to the vehicle chassis. In the physical universe, inertia never respects software timers. When the autonomy stack finally recognized an unavoidable collision at $T - 1.2\text{ s}$ with a remaining physical clearance of $d_{\text{clearance}} = 23.3\text{ m}$, the suppression logic withheld the braking command. During this one-second blackout window ($\Delta t_{\text{suppress}} = 1.0\text{ s}$), the vehicle accrued linear reaction travel debt:

$$d_{\text{react}} = v \cdot \Delta t_{\text{suppress}} = 19.4\text{ m/s} \times 1.0\text{ s} = 19.4\text{ m}$$

By coasting forward with zero decelerating force while the software timer counted down, the vehicle consumed $19.4\text{ m}$ of its available $23.3\text{ m}$ spatial buffer, leaving an unrecoverable residual clearance of only $d_{\text{remaining}} = d_{\text{clearance}} - d_{\text{react}} = 23.3\text{ m} - 19.4\text{ m} = 3.9\text{ m}$ when the timer finally expired at $T - 0.2\text{ s}$.

A basic kinematic analysis reveals why a catastrophic impact was physically unavoidable once the suppression window elapsed. Bringing a mass traveling at cruising velocity $v = 19.4\text{ m/s}$ to rest under maximum emergency mechanical braking deceleration ($a_{\text{max}} = \mu g \approx 0.8 \times 9.81\text{ m/s}^2 \approx 8.0\text{ m/s}^2$, governed by the tire-pavement Coulomb friction limit) requires a minimum quadratic braking distance:

$$d_{\text{brake}} = \frac{v^2}{2 a_{\text{max}}} = \frac{(19.4\text{ m/s})^2}{2 \times 8.0\text{ m/s}^2} = \frac{376.36}{16.0} \approx 23.5\text{ m}$$

The complete dynamic stopping envelope demands a total clearance of $d_{\text{stop}} = d_{\text{react}} + d_{\text{brake}} = 19.4\text{ m} + 23.5\text{ m} = 42.9\text{ m}$. With only $3.9\text{ m}$ of clearance remaining when the motion planner finally dispatched the brake command to the hydraulic actuators at $T - 0.2\text{ s}$, the vehicle possessed less than one-sixth of the required stopping distance. As detailed in the flight-recorder telemetry ledger (@tbl-telemetry-ch04), the vehicle struck the pedestrian at full cruising velocity ($19.4\text{ m/s}$) with zero automated braking deceleration applied, dissipating its entire kinetic energy ($3.8 \times 10^5\text{ J}$) into unmitigated physical destruction.

The enduring systems lesson of the Tempe collision is that safety-critical physical authority must never be subordinate to stochastic neural classifications or high-level software heuristics. In the Uber ATG architecture, the safety braking path was monolithic and centralized: the ability to execute an emergency stop depended on whether a complex, non-deterministic deep neural network correctly stabilized its semantic categories and whether an unverified user-space software timer expired. Physical AI demands a strict Proposal–Permission Boundary. High-level perception backbones and trajectory planners running on application processors (MPUs) or neural processing units (NPUs) at $10\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$ must be treated as untrusted advisory systems that generate candidate trajectory proposals. The authority to grant execution permission must reside strictly within an independent, class-agnostic safety reflex operating at a hard real-time $1000\text{ Hz}$ cadence on dedicated bare-metal microcontrollers (MCUs). This 1 kHz deterministic reflex continuously evaluates class-agnostic spatial occupancy bounds (derived directly from raw radar returns or direct time-of-flight sensors, completely bypassing the neural vision stack) against dynamic stopping equations ($d_{\text{clearance}} \ge d_{\text{stop}}$) in static SRAM with zero dynamic heap allocation (`malloc = 0`). Had such a multi-rate architecture been deployed, the class-agnostic 1 kHz safety monitor would have detected an occupied spatial volume at $T - 4.5\text{ s}$ and executed full regenerative and friction braking regardless of whether the high-level semantic model classified the obstacle as a car, a bicycle, or static clutter, arresting the vehicle dozens of meters before impact.


## The Three Cadences of Physical AI

The central architectural dilemma of embodied intelligence is that a physical agent cannot execute on a single, uniform computational clock without either sacrificing semantic reasoning capacity or compromising physical safety. In traditional cloud computing, software operates within an artificial, turn-based coordinate system: if a neural network experiences an unexpected garbage collection pause, cache miss storm, or memory bus stall, execution pauses behind a loading indicator while the digital universe patiently waits. In Physical AI, however, the physical universe serves as the unyielding master clock. While silicon deliberates, continuous dynamical equations govern reality: moving mass accumulates linear reaction debt $d_{\text{react}} = v \cdot \Delta t$, ungrounded linkages accelerate under gravity, and stator coils accumulate irreversible Joule heat. To bridge the four orders of magnitude separating high-level open-world comprehension from microsecond motor commutation, embodied architectures partition execution across three asynchronous temporal cadences: System 2 ($0.5\text{--}2\text{ Hz}$), System 1.5 ($20\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$), and System 1 ($1000\text{ Hz}$), illustrated in @fig-three-cadences and compared systematically across silicon and authority tiers in @tbl-three-cadences. This multi-rate hierarchy is governed by an uncompromising systems invariant: cognitive complexity is strictly decoupled from physical actuation privilege across an asynchronous Proposal–Permission boundary, ensuring that stochastic foundation models propose long-horizon behaviors without ever possessing direct hardware authority over actuator gate drivers.

![The Three Cadences of Physical AI. The asynchronous multi-rate temporal hierarchy: System 2 ($0.5\text{ to } 2\text{ Hz}$ Semantic Intent), System 1.5 ($20\text{ to } 50\text{ Hz}$ Action Chunking), and System 1 ($1000\text{ Hz}$ Real-Time Safety Reflex).](figures/fig03_three_cadences.svg){#fig-three-cadences width=100%}

### System 2: Semantic Deliberation

At the deliberative apex of the hierarchy operates System 2, executing at a deliberative cadence of $0.5\text{--}2\text{ Hz}$ (cycle periods $\Delta t \in [500, 2000]\text{ ms}$) on multi-core Linux Application Processors (MPUs) or offboard compute nodes. This tier ingests rich, high-bandwidth multimodal sensory streams (including multi-view RGB-D video, spatial point clouds, ambient acoustic signals, and natural language mission commands) to execute large Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models scaling from $7\text{B}$ to $70\text{B}$ parameters. Its primary computational role is open-world semantic affordance parsing, long-horizon symbolic task decomposition, and spatial reasoning across dynamic environments. Because deep autoregressive Transformer decoders suffer from stochastic execution latencies, heavy KV-cache memory bandwidth bottlenecks, and non-zero hallucination probabilities, System 2 occupies the privilege tier of an Untrusted Proposal Service. Rather than commanding raw joint angles, torques, or phase voltages, System 2 communicates exclusively by emitting structured Expiring Intent Leases, formally defined as:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{intent}} = \langle \mathcal{G}_{\text{task}}, \mathcal{S}_{\text{hull}}, t_{\text{issue}}, \Delta t_{\text{lease}}, \mathbf{w}_{\text{target}}, \mathcal{B}_{\text{keepout}} \rangle$$

where $\mathcal{G}_{\text{task}} \in \mathrm{SE}(3) \times \mathbb{R}^k$ encodes the semantic sub-goal (such as a 6-DoF end-effector target pose), $\mathcal{S}_{\text{hull}} \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ establishes a mathematically certified spatial operating hull bounding permissible linkage workspace, $t_{\text{issue}} \in \mathbb{R}^+$ denotes the hardware-synchronized PTP (Precision Time Protocol / IEEE 1588) timestamp of lease generation, $\Delta t_{\text{lease}} \in \mathbb{R}^+$ specifies a finite time-to-live validity duration (typically $50\text{--}200\text{ ms}$), $\mathbf{w}_{\text{target}} \in \mathbb{R}^6$ provides a target topological waypoint or desired operational-space contact wrench ($[F_x, F_y, F_z, \tau_x, \tau_y, \tau_z]^T$ in $\text{N}$ and $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$), and $\mathcal{B}_{\text{keepout}} \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ specifies dynamic obstacle volumes. 

To ground this mathematically, consider an autonomous manipulator inserting a battery cell: System 2 issues a lease specifying sub-goal $\mathcal{G}_{\text{task}} = [0.45, 0.10, 0.15]^T\text{ m}$, spatial hull $\mathcal{S}_{\text{hull}}$ as a cylinder of radius $r = 0.50\text{ m}$, timestamp $t_{\text{issue}} = 1718000000.120\text{ s}$, validity $\Delta t_{\text{lease}} = 100\text{ ms}$, nominal downward seating force $\mathbf{w}_{\text{target}} = [0, 0, -2.5\text{ N}, 0, 0, 0]^T$, and keep-out region $\mathcal{B}_{\text{keepout}}$ bounding the assembly fixture base ($z \le 0.0\text{ m}$). If an unexpected MPU garbage collection pause or CUDA kernel stall prevents System 2 from renewing the contract before $t_{\text{issue}} + \Delta t_{\text{lease}} = 1718000000.220\text{ s}$, the active lease expires deterministically, forcing downstream planners into a safe hold above the fixture without stalling the physical motor loops.

### System 1.5: Trajectory Decoding

Bridging the gap between discrete semantic intent and continuous mechanical motion is System 1.5, executing at a medium trajectory cadence of $20\text{ to } 50\text{ Hz}$ with cycle periods of $20\text{ to } 50\text{ ms}$ on dedicated Edge Neural Processing Units (NPUs) and pinned real-time Linux threads configured with `PREEMPT_RT` priority scheduling and `mlockall` address space locking to eliminate page faults. System 1.5 continuously ingests the active intent lease $\mathcal{L}_{\text{intent}}$ alongside high-rate proprioceptive state estimates $\mathbf{x}_t \in \mathbb{R}^n$ to decode continuous multi-step motion sequences using Action Chunking Transformers (ACT), Diffusion Policies, or real-time non-linear Model Predictive Control (MPC). Rather than emitting discrete single-step actions that amplify network jitter and latency instability, System 1.5 generates receding-horizon trajectory chunks $\tau_t = \{\mathbf{q}_{t+k}, \dot{\mathbf{q}}_{t+k}, \ddot{\mathbf{q}}_{t+k}\}_{k=1}^H$ spanning a predictive horizon of $H = 16$ waypoints. 

To prevent mechanical damage, System 1.5 fits and enforces $\mathcal{C}^2$ polynomial spline continuity across joint space, mathematically constraining the third time-derivative of position, joint jerk:

$$\dddot{\mathbf{q}}(t) = \frac{d^3 \mathbf{q}}{dt^3} \le \mathbf{j}_{\text{max}}$$

where $\mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ represents the joint coordinate vector in radians ($\text{rad}$), $\dot{\mathbf{q}}$ is angular velocity ($\text{rad/s}$), $\ddot{\mathbf{q}}$ is acceleration ($\text{rad/s}^2$), $\dddot{\mathbf{q}}$ is joint jerk ($\text{rad/s}^3$), and $\mathbf{j}_{\text{max}}$ is the maximum allowable jerk threshold. Without $\mathcal{C}^2$ continuity, commanding a step change in joint acceleration of $\Delta \ddot{q} = 20\text{ rad/s}^2$ across a single $1\text{ ms}$ discrete sample period generates an impulsive jerk of $\dddot{q} = 20{,}000\text{ rad/s}^3$. For a robot arm with joint inertia $J = 0.5\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$, this step discontinuity demands an instantaneous torque rate of $\dot{\tau} = J \dddot{q} = 10{,}000\text{ N}\cdot\text{m/s}$, launching acoustic shockwaves through mechanical transmissions, chipping planetary gear teeth, stripping harmonic drive flexsplines, and tripping inverter over-current protections. By enforcing $\dddot{\mathbf{q}}(t) \le \mathbf{j}_{\text{max}} = 100\text{ rad/s}^3$ via quintic splines, System 1.5 bounds dynamic torque rates to $\dot{\tau} \le 50\text{ N}\cdot\text{m/s}$, suppressing high-frequency impact stresses ($\sigma_{\text{contact}} \propto \dddot{\mathbf{q}}$) and eliminating inductive voltage spikes across stator windings. Operating as a Candidate Trajectory Generator, System 1.5 holds semi-trusted authority: its emitted waypoint chunks represent kinematically feasible and dynamically smooth proposals, but remain entirely subordinate to downstream real-time physical verification.

### System 1: Real-Time Reflexes

At the foundation of the physical AI hierarchy resides System 1, executing at a hard real-time reflex cadence of $1000\text{ Hz} \pm 5\,\mu\text{s}$ (a strict $1.0\text{ ms}$ loop period) on dedicated bare-metal microcontrollers, such as ARM Cortex-M7 or dual-core lockstep RISC-V cores. System 1 executes exclusively out of single-cycle Tightly Coupled Memory (ITCM/DTCM) and static SRAM under the strict mandate of Zero Dynamic Heap Allocation (`malloc = 0`), eliminating operating system context switches, translation lookaside buffer (TLB) misses, and memory fragmentation jitter. 

The requirement for $1000\text{ Hz}$ execution is rooted directly in frequency-domain control stability. In physical feedback control, any computational and communication delay $t_{\text{delay}}$ introduces an uncompensated phase lag proportional to the plant's crossover frequency $\omega_c$:

$$\Delta \phi = -\omega_c t_{\text{delay}} \cdot \frac{180^\circ}{\pi}$$

To understand phase lag intuitively, imagine steering a high-speed vehicle where the video display has a 200 ms rendering lag: when the car drifts right, by the time you observe it and steer left, the vehicle has already drifted further right; your delayed correction adds energy to the perturbation rather than damping it, sending the vehicle into wild fish-tailing oscillations. For a mechanical system with a responsive bandwidth of $\omega_c = 25\text{ rad/s}$ ($4\text{ Hz}$) and an available phase margin of $35^\circ$, a delay of $t_{\text{delay}} = 25\text{ ms}$ (typical of non-real-time Linux stacks) introduces $\Delta \phi \approx -35.8^\circ$, consuming the entire phase margin and flipping negative stabilizing feedback into destructive limit-cycle oscillations. By executing at $1000\text{ Hz}$ with $t_{\text{delay}} \le 1.0\text{ ms}$, System 1 restricts phase erosion to $\Delta \phi \le -1.4^\circ$, preserving robust stability margins across dynamic disturbances.

Operating as the Sole Hardware Permission Authority, System 1 mediates all communication between upstream trajectory generators and the $20\text{ kHz}$ Field-Oriented Control (FOC) inverter pulse-width modulation (PWM) gate drivers. Every millisecond tick, System 1 evaluates a minimal-intervention safety filter:

$$\mathbf{u}^* = \arg\min_{\mathbf{u} \in \mathcal{U}_{\text{safe}}} \frac{1}{2} \|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}\|^2 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \dot{h}(\mathbf{x}) \ge -\gamma h(\mathbf{x})$$

where $h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0$ defines a certified safe envelope (parameterized by active workspace hulls and obstacle keep-out bounds), $\mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}$ is the candidate torque proposed by System 1.5, and $\gamma > 0$ (with SI units of $\text{s}^{-1}$) acts as a forward speed governor: when distance to an obstacle is $h(\mathbf{x}) = d - d_{\text{min}}$, the condition enforces $v_{\text{approach}} = -\dot{h} \le \gamma (d - d_{\text{min}})$, smoothly throttling allowable approach velocity to zero at the boundary ($h(\mathbf{x}) \to 0$). For example, if $\gamma = 5.0\text{ s}^{-1}$ and the remaining clearance to an obstacle is $h = 0.10\text{ m}$ ($10\text{ cm}$), the barrier condition constrains the closing speed to $v_{\text{approach}} \le 5.0 \times 0.10 = 0.50\text{ m/s}$; when clearance shrinks to $h = 0.02\text{ m}$ ($2\text{ cm}$), allowable speed is throttled to $0.10\text{ m/s}$, reaching $0\text{ m/s}$ at the boundary ($h = 0$).^[The formal derivation of Control Barrier Functions, their Lie derivative expansion $L_f h(\mathbf{x}) + L_g h(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u} \ge -\alpha(h(\mathbf{x}))$, and their real-time quadratic programming implementation on microcontrollers are developed in @sec-enforcement.] 

Within this sub-millisecond evaluation budget, System 1 continuously verifies dynamic stopping clearance:

$$d_{\text{clearance}} \ge d_{\text{stop}}(v) = v \cdot \tau_{\text{latency}} + \frac{v^2}{2 a_{\text{max}}}$$

where $v$ is instantaneous velocity ($\text{m/s}$), $\tau_{\text{latency}}$ is worst-case sensing transport latency ($\text{s}$), and $a_{\text{max}}$ is maximum emergency deceleration ($\text{m/s}^2$). For a robot moving at $v = 1.5\text{ m/s}$ with sensing latency $\tau_{\text{latency}} = 50\text{ ms}$ and braking limit $a_{\text{max}} = 3.0\text{ m/s}^2$, reaction drift burns $v \tau = 0.075\text{ m}$ ($7.5\text{ cm}$) and quadratic deceleration requires $v^2 / (2a_{\text{max}}) = 0.375\text{ m}$ ($37.5\text{ cm}$), requiring a minimum clearance of $d_{\text{stop}} = 0.45\text{ m}$ ($45\text{ cm}$). Concurrently, System 1 superimposes closed-loop impedance regulation $\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{K}_p(\mathbf{q}_{\text{ref}} - \mathbf{q}) + \mathbf{D}(\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{\text{ref}} - \dot{\mathbf{q}})$ (where stiffness $\mathbf{K}_p$ in $\text{N}\cdot\text{m/rad}$ acts as a virtual mechanical spring and damping $\mathbf{D}$ in $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s/rad}$ acts as a virtual dashpot) alongside dynamic contact damping $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{damp}} = -\mathbf{D} \dot{\mathbf{q}}$ to guarantee passivity and dissipate collision kinetic energy during unexpected physical contact, dynamically clamping or projecting candidate actions into certified safe torque envelopes before energizing motor phase windings.

| :--- | :--- | :---: | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |

| **System 1.5** | Trajectory Planning & Action Chunking | $20\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$ ($20\text{--}50\text{ ms}$) | Edge NPU / Tensor Core GPU | Real-time Linux (`PREEMPT_RT`) / C++ / TensorRT | $\mathcal{C}^2$ Spline Waypoint Chunks ($H=16$, $\dddot{\mathbf{q}} \le \mathbf{j}_{\text{max}}$) | Semi-trusted (Candidate Trajectory Generator) |
